Polaris RZR Pro R Factory Boost Will Thunder Through the Desert with 400 HP and a $200K Sticker
13 photos
Photo: Polaris
Next year's desert racing season could look a bit different than it used to be if American powersports company Polaris has its way, and the new variant of the RZR side-by-side snatches the minds and pockets of racers.
Called the RZR Pro R Factory Boost, Polaris' newest insanity brings together the enhancements announced earlier in the summer for the RZR Pro R Boost and the RZR Pro R Factory, and what resulted is simply mind-boggling.
Built on a reinforced chassis, the Factory Boost throws in a wheelbase that's 6.5 inches (16.5 cm) longer than before, now at 111 inches (282 cm). It is now fitted with larger tubes across structural members, so that it can take a beating in the open desert races it will most definitely be part of soon.
Because the side-by-side has been imagined with competitions in mind, its ProStar Fury 2.0-liter engine is not to be taken lightly. Tuned for racing, the four-cylinder cranks out 400 horsepower. That's the same as the RZR Pro R Factory it will soon join, but a lot more than this summer's Boost model, which is only good for 275 horsepower.
The engine draws fuel from a 45-gallon (170-liter) fuel cell, larger than on the base model (which stands at 34 gallons/128 liters) and good for as many as 200 miles (322 km). All of that, as well as an all-new cage, is hidden under a limited carbon fiber bodywork that wraps around a slightly wider cabin –two inches (five cm).
For suspension, the Polaris RZR Pro R Factory Boost uses three-inch (7.6 cm) internal bypass Dynamix DV shocks that have been modified with race-specific components, while a standard Fox steering damper makes sure steering and control are just right.
Finally, Polaris throws in on its new desert racer a fully integrated MoTeC electronics package that comprises, among other things, an upgraded ECU, dual power distribution modules, and a second PDM.
The company presented its new vehicle during the annual Camp RZR event at Glamis Imperial Sand Dunes in California, which took place this past weekend. From there, the new vehicle went straight to Polaris' configurator, where it is now listed as available.
There will be a limited window for people to order their new desert racer, which closes in mid-February 2026. Polaris is asking $200,000 for it, but that's only the minimum, as speccing it differently from stock will cost more.
For the record, the Polaris RZR Pro R Boost that was shown this summer came with an asking price of only $49,999.
Before it gets into customer hands, Polaris will take the Pro R Factory Boost out for a spin in the hands of its own factory team during the 2027 King of the Hammers event that takes place in mid-January in California.

Europe is preparing to introduce a new requirement that could change how electric bicycle batteries are tracked, repaired, recycled, and potentially even resold. Starting in February 2027, new e-bike batteries sold in the European Union will be required to carry a digital battery passport, giving each battery its own digital identity and making important information about its origins and characteristics accessible throughout its lifetime.
And while the rules are European, their impact could eventually reach American e-bike riders, too.
The battery passport requirement comes from the EU’s 2023 Batteries Regulation , which established new standards for battery sustainability, traceability, and transparency. The rules cover several categories of batteries, including those used in electric cars, electric bicycles, electric scooters, and other light electric vehicles.
Beginning February 18, 2027, newly placed batteries in these categories will need digital passports accessible through QR codes. Scanning the code will provide access to information about the battery, though exactly what users can see will depend on their authorization level.

The information can include details such as the battery’s manufacturer, chemistry, capacity, cycle count, carbon footprint, and materials used in its construction. The system also provides for information about battery performance and durability, including data related to battery health and degradation.
That last part could be particularly interesting for electric bicycle owners.
What does this mean for e-bike riders?
Anyone who has purchased a used electric bicycle knows that the battery is often one of the biggest unknowns. A bike might look nearly new, but its battery could have hundreds of charge cycles under its belt and significantly reduced capacity.
Even a quick test ride before a secondhand e-bike purchase may fail to demonstrate just how little capacity remains in a heavily used battery.
With replacement e-bike batteries costing hundreds of dollars, that’s a pretty important detail.
The battery passport system could eventually help address that problem by making battery information more transparent. However, there’s an important distinction: the regulations don’t necessarily guarantee that everyday consumers will be able to scan a QR code and immediately see a battery’s remaining health percentage. Some of that information may be restricted to authorized users.
Even so, the system could help repair shops, recyclers, and secondhand buyers better understand the batteries they’re dealing with.
It could also make life more complicated for e-bike manufacturers, especially smaller brands that will now need to ensure their batteries meet the new documentation and traceability requirements.
What about electric bikes in the US?
There’s currently no equivalent nationwide battery passport requirement for electric bicycles in the United States, but that doesn’t mean American riders won’t eventually benefit.
Many major e-bike manufacturers sell their products in both Europe and North America. US-based companies like Trek and Specialized have major markets in Europe, and will have to comply with the new law. Chinese companies and other Asian manufacturers will also need to produce compliant batteries. Once those companies have developed systems to track individual batteries and provide digital passports for their European products, they may find it easier to extend those systems to their American models rather than maintain entirely separate processes.
That doesn’t mean US-bound batteries will automatically receive passports, but it could create an interesting spillover effect.
And considering how expensive e-bike batteries can be, anything that makes it easier to understand their condition, verify their origins, or facilitate repairs could be a welcome development.
For now, Europe is leading the charge on battery transparency. But if the system proves useful, American e-bike riders might eventually get some of the same benefits without waiting for Washington to catch up.

The Pacific Maritime Association and International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26 have signed a contract extension through 5 p.m. Pacific Time on Wednesday, Nov. 4, temporarily postponing a potential work stoppage at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach while negotiations continue.
The two sides will continue bargaining with assistance from the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service. The agreement provides additional time for talks but does not resolve the underlying labor dispute.
Local 26 represents approximately 250 watchmen who perform security-related duties at port terminals. According to PMA, those facilities handle roughly 85% of cargo moving through the Port of Long Beach and 33% at the Port of Los Angeles.
PMA said it remains committed to reaching a fair agreement at the bargaining table and avoiding disruption at the two ports, the busiest U.S. container hubs.
The watchmen’s previous agreement expired in July 2025, and employees have continued working under extensions while the union and employers negotiate a replacement. Local 26 members had authorized a potential strike ahead of the previous Nov. 1 deadline, according to PMA.
In an Oct. 23 letter, Local 26 President Luisa Gratz said negotiations with employers and PMA had been underway since 2025 without producing an agreement.
The union members earn an average of $170,000 a year. The sides hasn’t disclosed exact issues in the negotiations.
The watchmen’s negotiations are separate from the broader West Coast longshore labor agreement, which runs through 2028 and covers approximately 22,000 workers at 29 ports.
Although the watchmen account for about 2% of the ILWU workforce at the two ports, their role at major terminals creates the potential for a wider disruption. PMA has warned that other ILWU members could honor picket lines in the event of a strike, potentially interrupting vessel, yard and gate operations at affected facilities.
Why it matters: The extension gives negotiators more time to resolve a dispute involving about 250 watchmen at terminals handling substantial shares of Los Angeles and Long Beach cargo.

© Rehman Asad
By Bangladesh correspondent
2 November 2026
Bangladesh’s garment shippers face missed sailings and mounting pressure on delivery schedules as labour protests halt production and disrupt cargo movements to Chittagong port.
Production was suspended at around 690 garment factories today, according to the latest information from Bangladesh, while roadblocks hampered the movement of export cargo from Dhaka factories to the port.
The disruption threatens shipment schedules on two fronts: factories may struggle to complete orders on time; and finished garments face delays reaching their booked vessels.
For forwarders, prolonged unrest could mean rearranging collections and bookings as cargo readiness dates slip. Shipments missing sailing cut-offs could face longer delays, while buyers seeking to protect delivery deadlines may have to consider more-expensive airfreight.
However, there was no confirmed estimate of cargo delays, missed sailings, or additional demand for air transport as yet.
Workers continued demonstrations on Monday in Dhaka’s Mirpur area, Ashulia, Gazipur, and Tongi, demanding a new minimum wage and improved working conditions. Police and Border Guard Bangladesh personnel were deployed, with clashes reported with protesters.
Factory owners have threatened indefinite closures if the protests continue, raising the prospect of further disruption to production and exports.
Fazlee Shamim Ehsan, president of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association, said the unrest was already affecting overseas trade, and added: “Moreover, the ongoing labour movement is hampering production and exports. Buyers are worried.”
He warned that the disruption coincided with uncertainty already present in Bangladesh’s largest apparel market.
“Our largest market, Europe, is going through severe instability. As a result, European buyers will obviously purchase less now then in the past.”
Gazipur Industrial Police superintendent Amjad Hossain said more than 150 factories in his area had closed today because of the protests, and the nationwide closure figure rose during the day, the latest tally putting suspended production at around 690 factories. At least 500 factories had closed on Sunday amid fears of vandalism.
The government had formed a new wage board yesterday, headed by a district judge and included representatives of factory owners and workers, to determine a new minimum wage.
Workers are seeking a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000, approximately $250. Their other demands include food rationing in garment factories, implementation of trade union rights, a judicial investigation into workers’ deaths, and an end to unjustified lay-offs.
The formation of the board brought no immediate end to the demonstrations, with roadblocks and factory closures forming.
For garment buyers and their logistics providers, the immediate uncertainty is when factories can resume production and whether completed orders can reach the port in time.
Any extended shutdown would leave less room to recover lost production and transport time before contractual delivery deadlines.

Michael Strahan Bought This Dodge Challenger SRT Demon in 2023, Drove 350 Miles, Listed It for Sale
30 photos
Photo: Bring a Trailer
This car was "built especially for Michael Strahan." This is what the window sticker shows. Ordered directly by the Hall of Fame defensive end, this 2023 Dodge Challenger SRT Demon 170 Jailbreak Last Call (good luck remembering this designation!) is a one-of-one machine. Its one and only owner so far drove only 347 miles and listed it for sale.
What sets this Demon 170 apart from any other Demon 170 on the planet is a mix of exclusivity. So, first things first. The car features a custom factory plaque and serial number #00092, specially chosen by the NFL star to match the jersey number he wore throughout his entire 15-year career with the New York Giants.
Available by invitation only to an elite group of VIP customers, the Challenger Demon 170 Jailbreak Last Call was the swan song of an entire generation of muscle cars and cost an additional $29,995 on a first-come, first-served basis, unlocking access to 40 exclusive paint colors. This means that out of the entire production run, this is the sole example finished in Dark Green (paint code F8).
It features aggressively styled Satin Black graphics across the hood, roof, decklid, and taillight panel, while the Air Grabber hood carries the "Alcohol Injected" lettering. The Dodge Challenger SRT Demon 170 Jailbreak Last Call rides on Lacks Enterprises carbon fiber wheels, measuring 18 inches up front and 17 inches out back, wrapped in street-legal, drag-ready Mickey Thompson tires.
Photo: Bring a Trailer Michael Strahan's Challenger SRT Demon 170 comes with factory “01 of 01” and “Last Call” plaques, while another under the hood and the window sticker indicate that it was "built especially for Michael Strahan." He paid $162,836 to go home with it, with over $88,000 in factory options.
The option list includes the heated and ventilated front seats in Black Alcantara and Laguna leather with Demonic Red seatbelts, the Alcantara-wrapped multifunction steering wheel with shift paddles, and the plush suede headliner and door panel accents.
The 18-speaker Harman Kardon surround sound system, backed by a GreenEdge amplifier and a trunk-mounted subwoofer, is also on the list, as if the HEMI-diehard driver would ever need any other soundtrack outside that provided by the HEMI orchestra.
However, he didn't really enjoy it much, because now, three years after delivery, it only has 347 miles (558 kilometers) on the clock, which makes it a pristine, collector-grade machine that still has the factory yellow scuff guards attached to the front splitter and protective plastic foil on the screens inside the cabin.
Photo: Bring a Trailer Strahan probably saw it as an investment right from the get-go, hoping to cash in one day. That is such a pity, considering that the Demon 170 is the most powerful road-going car that Dodge has ever built before pulling the plug on the almighty HEMI and the cars that came with it.
..
That almighty 6.2-liter HEMI V8 works alongside a massive 3.0-liter supercharger with a 3.02” pulley and a 105-millimeter throttle body to pump out a mind-blowing 1,025 horsepower (1,039 metric horsepower) and 945 pound-feet (1,281 Newton meters) of torque on E85. That’s something that those buying a new-generation Dodge Charger Daytona or a Hurricane-powered Charger can only dream of.
It is a bit tamer when running on regular pump gas, with a factory rating of 900 horsepower (912 metric horsepower) and 810 pound-feet (1,098 Newton meters) of torque. On E85, it rockets from zero to hero (0 to 60 mph or 0 to 97 kph) in just 1.66 seconds, runs the quarter mile in a staggering 8.91 seconds at 151.17 mph (243.28 kph) and maxes out (don't laugh!) at 149 mph (240 kph). Yeah, right.
An eight-speed TorqueFlite automatic transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels in pure muscle car fashion. Black-painted four-piston Brembo brake calipers, sporting the yellow "SRT" lettering over ventilated discs, provide the stopping power. The Demon rides on an edition-specific Drag Mode suspension with adaptive damping shocks and features Launch Control to make it rocket down the strip.
Photo: Bring a Trailer The 2023 Dodge Challenger SRT Demon Jailbreak Last Call is now going with a clean Montana title and a clean Carfax report with no accidents or mileage discrepancies. Who would have thought, right? The winning bidder will get the ultimate collector documentation pack.
The orientation kit brings the color samples of the 40 exclusive paint options available, the custom Demon 170 drinkware set, and the elite wooden presentation chest with the VIN and the owner’s name engraved, housing the printed signatures of the entire Dodge Design Team. The original window sticker and the owner’s manual are also included.
The auction on Bring a Trailer will end on Thursday, November 5. With three days to go, bidding got as far as $89,400. That surely is light-years away from what the owner hopes to get for the HEMI-powered monster that he bought back in 2023 and hardly ever touched.
Hopefully, even though owners prefer to keep such cars low mileage , hoping their value rockets over the years, whoever buys it will track it until its wheels fall off.

© Iqoncept
By Charlotte Goldstone
2 November 2026
Global schedule reliability has become more seasonal, while weekly liner service deployments have grown increasingly volatile since the pandemic, according to new analysis by Sea-Intelligence.
Drawing on its Global Liner Performance database, which tracks monthly vessel arrivals from July 2011 to September 2026, the consultant found a stronger relationship between declining punctuality and the severity of delays, at , alongside more pronounced seasonal fluctuations in reliability.
While declining reliability has historically been associated with longer delays, the correlation between the two measures has shifted to a lower sustained level since the pandemic, indicating a tighter relationship between whether vessels arrive late and the magnitude of their delays than was evident before.
Source: Sea-Intelligence
Sea-Intelligence also identified a marked change in the seasonal pattern of global schedule reliability.
Before the pandemic, between 2013 and 2019, reliability typically fell in the early months of the year, improved through spring and early summer, dipped slightly in late summer, before reaching another peak in October and November.
Source: Sea-Intelligence
However, the alignment of individual years with this established seasonal pattern has deteriorated since 2020.
Source: Sea-Intelligence
Comparing average monthly reliability across the two periods, Sea-Intelligence found that seasonal fluctuations have become more pronounced, with lower reliability at the start of the year and higher performance peaks during the summer. The consultant said the overall pattern had become more extreme compared with pre-pandemic conditions.
Source: Sea-Intelligence
Separate Sea-Intelligence analysis found that the number of weekly services operated on the main Asia-Europe and transpacific trades had become considerably more volatile.
Using its Trade Capacity Outlook database, Sea-Intelligence measured weekly service numbers on four major routes: Asia-North America West Coast; Asia-North America East Coast; Asia-North Europe; and Asia-Mediterranean.
The analysis accounted for fluctuations caused by new service launches and cancellations, blank sailings, schedule slippage, and seasonal or niche services. To measure changes in operational consistency, the consultant calculated the annual standard deviation in weekly service numbers as a percentage of the average number of services operated.
The results showed a clear upward shift from 2020 across all four trades, indicating greater uncertainty about how many services would actually operate from one week to the next.
The increase was particularly pronounced on the Asia-Europe routes, where variability rose more sharply than on the transpacific.
Comparing average variability in 2013-2019 with 2020-2026, Sea-Intelligence found that Asia-North America East Coast experienced the smallest increase, at 26%, while Asia-North Europe recorded the largest, at 78%.
The findings have implications beyond the planning challenges faced by cargo owners and logistics providers, as greater week-to-week fluctuations in service numbers also make it harder for container terminals to plan resources and manage workloads, as the number of vessels and volume of cargo requiring handling can change significantly.
Sea-Intelligence warned that this increased the risk of sudden congestion, which could, in turn, undermine schedule reliability further.

Wondering how long your new electric car might last? This 2019 Chevrolet Bolt EV is proving that electric vehicles can rack up miles with the best of them – and its owner is committed to taking it past the half million mile mark.
You’d think a 250,000 mile Ford Mustang Mach-E maintaining 92% of its battery life , a 360,000 mile Hyundai IONIQ 5 with 87% battery health still intact , and a half-dozen stories of Tesla Model S , 3, and Y ride share vehicles racking up six figures on their odometers later would do more to convince the slow adopters and doubting Thomases of the world that EV batteries are built to last. The good news is that the evidence keeps piling up, and this latest example of electric endurance is a good one.
On the Out of Spec Renew YouTube channel , the crew took in a 2019 Chevy Bolt EV – one of the most affordable new EVs you could buy in 2019 – that had more than 470,000 miles on the clock and 330,000 miles on its post-recall battery. That’s nearly half a million miles on the original electric motor, and it’s still got more to go.
Out of Spec Renew replaced the 2019’s battery pack that was experiencing serious battery faults and cell-voltage imbalances with a stable, lower-mile example from a 2017 model. Once it was up and in, they got the car powered up, programmed, and driving again, putting the owner on track to reach the 500,000 mile milestone (sorry) in their trusty steed .

By Alex Lennane
2 November 2026
Disruption to ocean shipping is not triggering a large-scale switch to airfreight – the cost of emergency lift is keeping most shippers at sea, according to DSV.
Speaking at TIACA’s Air Cargo Forum in Miami last week, head of global airfreight Achim Martinka said such decisions depended on whether the business impact of a delay justified paying the airfreight premium.
“Most of the customers still stay on the seafreight side because they are not used to having shipments on time anyway,” he said. “If you have two or three weeks’ delay, this is a normal thing. And if you would switch to airfreight, it could be up to 20 times more expensive. So this is really a very tough financial decision to take.”
Conversion volumes remained limited, he said and added: “The conversion to air is still not in huge numbers. It’s still on a lower level, from what we see.”
But shippers that wait too long before seeking an alternative risk are finding any available airfreight capacity has become prohibitively expensive.
“Usually, our contracts are already signed for six or 12 months with the airlines. So everything which comes on a spontaneous, ad hoc basis will be even more expensive than the base load already on the aircraft,” Mr Martinka explained.
Where the duration of a disruption was uncertain, he said, shippers needed to begin arranging an airfreight solution.
“Otherwise, you’re going to be the last one, and then capacity is not affordable anymore.”
The competition to secure lift is also evident at Atlas Air, where Martin Drew, chief strategy and transformation officer, told The Loadstar forwarders and shippers increasingly wanted the certainty of dedicated capacity.
“The contract durations we have are very lengthy, because forwarders, in particular, and shippers want that capacity locked-in,” he said. “It helps from a planning perspective, knowing they’ve got that capacity, especially in an environment where supply is constrained.”
Atlas itself has demand for dedicated aircraft it cannot currently accommodate. Mr Drew said: “We’ve got a pipeline today of business that is tens of aircraft, and we can’t service that demand.”
However, finding space is only one obstacle to switching modes. Mr Martinka warned that ocean shipments required new documentation and operational preparation, including checks on dangerous goods, aircraft dimensions, and how cargo would need to be rebuilt for flight.
The practical difficulties were illustrated by Emir Pineda, director of air service development at Miami-Dade Aviation Department, who described an attempt to establish a sea-air movement of Honduran okra to the UK via Miami and Amsterdam.
“We were able to get a permit from USDA to transport perishable product from Central America via ship to Miami, then take it from Miami, without opening it, to the airport and then put it on an airplane and fly it to Europe. Sounds pretty simplistic, but it was actually quite complicated.
“It got to Miami: two containers – that’s a lot of cargo for one airplane.
“We had to find the capacity on a freighter, because it had to go all in one shipment [and the] capacity had to be available on the day the ship was arriving, because you only had two days to move it. Those were the conditions USDA set.
“We also had to maintain the cool chain throughout the logistics supply chain, because it had to keep a certain temperature.
“Once it got to Amsterdam, refrigerated trucks trucked it over to the UK. In the end, it worked. One time.
“Why only one time? Because of the complexity behind that. You had to get a shipper to agree to get it on the ship to Miami, and then you had to find the capacity on a consistent basis to move 60 tonnes for several weeks.
“What do you tell that customer when the season’s over? ‘Could you bring back the freight?’,” asked Mr Pineda. “That doesn’t work for forwarders; they want consistency. They want capacity availability when they need it.”
Mr Martinka said most shippers had developed some form of emergency plan since Covid, but he was not seeing a regular shift of ocean volumes into airfreight simply to maintain a contingency route.
“It is certainly a part of a resilience plan, which perhaps needs to be tested from time to time,” he said.
Forwarders and airlines had, nevertheless, become faster at adapting their networks to disruption, he added. DSV’s ACMI capacity allowed it to change destinations when customers needed alternatives.
“We have our own network, so we can decide every day with our ACMI flights where to fly. We can switch immediately if that’s needed for the customer.
“The good thing in air cargo is that airfreight is like water: it’s going to find its way.”

By Nils Roche
2 November 2026
After two ambitious Chinese-backed infrastructure projects were abandoned or stalled, Sierra Leone is turning to another Chinese partner to develop a “national” shipping industry. The financing model has changed, but familiar questions remain.
On 19 October, Sierra Leone inaugurated its new national shipping company, Sierra Leone Ocean Shipping Company (SLOSCO), with ambitions to operate, in time, 50 vessels and capture a significant share of the country’s maritime trade.
The venture is 70% owned by China’s Zhejiang Xiehai Group, with the remaining 30% held by the state-owned Sierra Leone National Shipping Agency (SLNSA).
The objective is straightforward: retain more of the freight earnings generated by Sierra Leone’s imports and mineral exports.
But the country has a history of ambitious Chinese-backed transport investments that failed to materialise.
Non-events
In November 2017, ICBC and China Eximbank agreed to finance a $659m expansion of Freetown’s Queen Elizabeth II Quay, backed by a sovereign guarantee.
The project’s financial viability was questionable. Its repayment structure depended partly on port-related revenues, potentially increasing costs for shipping lines and cargo owners.
The project stalled following the 2018 change of government.
In September 2026, an investigation by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists revealed that ICBC had committed to financing before completing its due diligence. Subsequent compliance checks identified corruption allegations involving individuals connected to the developer.
ICBC ultimately decided not to disburse its financing, according to the investigation. The allegations were rejected by the developer’s representatives.
Another Chinese-backed project suffered a similar fate. In 2018, Sierra Leone cancelled the proposed $318m Mamamah International Airport after concluding that the investment was economically unjustifiable, particularly given the underutilisation of the existing airport.
Both cases demonstrated the risks of pursuing ambitious infrastructure development without sufficiently convincing commercial foundations.
Today?
SLOSCO is fundamentally different in one respect: it is structured as an equity joint-venture, rather than a sovereign-guaranteed infrastructure loan.
Xiehai is an established shipping operator with a fleet of 42 vessels and a commercial network. This potentially allows SLOSCO to enter the market without purchasing dozens of vessels or accumulating substantial public debt.
Yet the distinction between vessels actually owned by SLOSCO, those chartered from Xiehai, and ships merely managed commercially remains unclear.
More importantly, the Sierra Leone National Shipping Agency Act 2025 grants the national carrier discretionary rights concerning the transportation of 40% of the value of the country’s imports and exports.
That could be more commercially significant than the fleet itself.
But cargo value is not freight revenue, and statutory rights do not necessarily translate into actual shipping contracts. Much of Sierra Leone’s mineral trade involves international commodity buyers and exporters who may already control vessel nominations.
The question is whether SLOSCO can compete commercially or will depend on preferential access to cargo.
Illicit cargo?
At this point we have to also refer to the well-documented case of Dutch drug trafficker Jos Leijdekkers, who is Sierra Leone president Julius Bio, and who has established the country as a key hub in the transport of cocaine from South America to Europe.
These are not merely allegations – Dutch courts have sentenced Leijdekkers in absentia to over 100 years in prison for several murders, while this excellent Guardian report details the extraordinary lengths that he has gone to using established shipping routes (and companies, for shipping industry folk it’s a roll-call of household names and really is a must-read for anyone trying to understand how licit and illicit cargoes intersect) from Freetown to ship drugs to Europe.
Which means there is a possibility that the SLOSCO project could, in part, be an attempt to create a legitimate business to cover the doings of an illegitimate one…
But that aside…
Sierra Leone’s ambition to retain maritime earnings is understandable. However, freight revenues must cover vessel operating costs, charter hire, financing and insurance, while 70% of the company’s equity belongs to its Chinese partner.
The country may still benefit substantially through employment, taxes, dividends and maritime expertise.
For Sierra Leone, the decisive test will not be whether SLOSCO reaches 50 vessels or secures a statutory share of cargo. It will be whether the arrangement delivers competitive freight services, sustainable returns and measurable economic value for the country.
After the unfulfilled port expansion and the abandoned airport, Sierra Leone has an opportunity to demonstrate that it has learned from experience.
This time, the ships may already exist. The question is whether the business model can stand on its own.

2013 Honda CBR1000RR Fireblade in Repsol Overalls Has Been With James May for 7 Years, Selling Cheap
13 photos
Photo: Collecting Cars
Every now and then, celebrities try to get rid of some of the vehicles they own, and they often turn to auction houses to handle the job. It's an opportunity for them to make some money, and for their fans to own something that belonged to their idol. And that's exactly what happened for people with a passion for James May and his dealings, who had a pretty exciting couple of weeks.
First, their hearts started pumping a bit faster in October, when James May listed for sale a 1974 Triumph Stag MKII. Not just any Stag , but the very one the British presenter drove in the final episode of The Grand Tour.
May went for online bidding to get rid of it, and the Stag didn't disappoint: it rapidly found a new owner, someone who chose to pay 37,100 pounds (almost $50,000 at today's exchange rates) for it. For reference, that's a lot more than the 25,000 pounds ($33,000) other Stags in good condition go for.
There's no need for me to tell you that May has always been a car nut, and that we'll probably see some more of his four-wheeled possessions pop up for sale in the near future. But the man is also passionate about motorcycles, and that's what brings us here now.
More specifically, it's a Honda CBR1000RR Fireblade that does that, as it is now selling. Not just any other Fireblade, but one from the Repsol run that has been in May's garage for seven years.
The superbike carries all the original mechanical bits, including the frame, 998cc inline-four engine, and six-speed transmission. It shows just 5,844 miles (9,400 km) of use since it first rolled off the lines, but it's unclear how much James May contributed to that.
The bike carries the orange and black Repsol racing livery, highlighted by red and white detailing, but also Honda and Repsol branding. After all, when it was first made, it wanted to honor the many Honda MotoGP successes, and these colors were the best way to do that.
Like all others of its kind, the machine comes with all of the original bodywork, including fairings and fuel tank. The suspension system is Showa (front forks and rear monoshock), while the braking hardware comes from Tokico.
May says the motorcycle has always been kept in a dry environment, but that didn't prevent the orange of the bodywork from fading slightly. If that's not a problem (and it shouldn't be), the buyer will get the bike accompanied by the service book, owner's handbook, and the V5C registration certificate. Why, there are even paddock-stand bobbins thrown into the mix.
The online auction for the James May 2013 Honda CBR1000RR Fireblade Repsol went live a while back, and the most someone is willing to pay for it is £9,300, or almost $12,500. There are around 31 hours left in the bidding process at the time of writing.

Toyota's Hybrid Minivan Gets Recalls, 228K Sienna People Carriers Affected Stateside
14 photos
Photo: Toyota / edited
In the world of automotive seatbelts, the pretensioner has one clear job, and that is to pull the belt tight during a crash. This keeps the occupant in place, minimizing the risk of injury. As far as certain Sienna hybrids are concerned, that pull can make the second-row seat recliner mechanism oscillate until its locking mechanism disengages.
This concern prompted a recall totaling 228,367 vehicles in the US market, namely Sienna minivans produced for model years 2022 through 2026. For North America, the Sienna is proudly assembled by Toyota Motor Manufacturing Indiana on the GA-K platform that underpins the Highlander twins. Over in China, two joint ventures produce the Sienna in Guangzhou and Tianjin, respectively.
Regarding the US-market recall population, the failure requires a specific combination of pretensioner timing, seat back movement, and frontal crash forces for the second-row seats to fold when they should not. Toyota identified this combination while investigating seat assemblies, reproducing the condition as part of internal crash testing.
Although the pretensioner does exactly what it's expected to do, the forces it generates can interfere with the mechanism that holds the seat back upright. Each second-row seat has an integrated seatbelt and pretensioner, and said pretensioner is designed to retract the belt in the event of a crash. The seat back, meanwhile, uses an outboard recliner mechanism with interlocking teeth.
When the pretensioner deploys, the load from its deployment creates oscillation between the recliner's cam and pawls. In combination with relative seat back displacement, pretensioner deployment timing, and frontal crash pulses, the cam may rotate far enough to disengage the recliner from the locked position. This, in turn, allows the seat back to move during a crash.
Photo: Toyota TMNA started looking into this matter back in January 2025, when a modified seat assembly and a modified seatbelt assembly were tested for a future production-intent model. During sled tests, the outboard recliner disengaged. Through August 2026, the company ran additional tests to isolate the variables. Toyota Motor North America further recovered second-row seat assemblies from the field to check the condition of the recliners.
Full vehicle crash tests followed suit between September and October 2026, and those crash tests helped Toyota reproduce the conditions it had previously identified on the sled. Internally referred to as 26V690 by the NHTSA , this recall comprises Sienna hybrids assembled from September 16, 2021, through July 20, 2026.
Toyota Boshoku Indiana is listed in the recall documentation as the seat assembly supplier. The remedy splits the recall population into two groups. For approximately 200 units equipped with the Mobility as a Service Package, both second-row seat backs will be replaced in full. The replacements feature a different recliner mechanism.
The remaining vehicle population will be fixed through software, with Toyota instructing dealers to install updated SRS electronic control unit software. Known customers will be notified by first-class mail no later than December 21, 2026.

Kimi Antonelli Is a Formula 1 World Champion. Now What?
10 photos
Photo: Mercedes-AMG F1 Team/Getty Images
Back in May, I wrote an extensive editorial regarding the possible fallout from Kimi Antonelli becoming a World Champion so early in his Formula 1 career. I argued that while he is obviously an extraordinary talent, I still wouldn't bet money on Formula 1 benefiting from crowning someone so young, so fast.
Well, here we are. Antonelli is officially the champ, and I suppose I owe the kid an apology. Or at least an explanation.
At just 20-years-old, Kimi shattered Sebastian Vettel's record as the youngest champion in F1 history. He's also the first Italian to win the title since Alberto Ascari did it in 1953, thus ending a 73-year drought. He's done all this in only his second season, which was about as unlikely as, I don't know... it was unlikely. I didn't think it would happen. Not this year, anyway.
Like most of you, I figured George Russell would eventually close the gap, or that Max would mount one of his ridiculous comebacks. But it wasn't to be. Antonelli wrapped up the title fight with four races still left to go.
The problem with winning too soon My original argument had nothing to do with Kimi's talent. I've never questioned his skills as a top F1 prospect. It was more about the way we perceive greatness in Formula 1, and how much of that perception depends on the journey rather than the destination. Look at the likes of Michael Schumacher, Fernando Alonso, or Max Verstappen. All of them had to establish themselves against formidable opposition before becoming dominant.
They were never blessed with a title-winning car right off the bat. To be fair, Hamilton came really close to winning the title as a rookie in 2007, before claiming it the following year. His and Kimi's career look pretty similar from that standpoint - even though Kimi did not come close to winning it all in his rookie season.
Still, he went from being a promising débutant to world champion in what feels like 5 minutes. It's almost unfair. We've barely had any time to appreciate him as a prospect and suddenly we're celebrating him as best-of-the-best. Then again, we're probably witnessing something even scarier than that - a world champion who hasn't even hit his ceiling yet, which I think we all know is true.
The Mercedes factor There's no escaping the fact that Mercedes entered the new regulatory era with by far the most competitive package. They've been on top for most of the season, I'd say, with Ferrari and Red Bull catching up after the summer break. So yes, Antonelli benefited greatly from that performance advantage, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest.
Photo: Mercedes-AMG F1 Team/Getty Images The flip side of that argument is that every great F1 champion has had championship-winning machinery. Schumacher with his Ferraris, Hamilton with his hybrid-era Mercs, Vettel and Max with their Red Bulls, and so on. However, my argument stands - Antonelli didn't spend years establishing himself as the best driver on the grid before getting the chance to drive a title-winning car.
So, from that standpoint, I think his achievement isn't as impressive as what Max did in 2021, or what Michael did in 1994 when his Benetton was quite inferior to the Williams of that era.
But I guess I'm just going to keep playing devil's advocate here. Russell has been driving the exact same car as Kimi, and despite his experience, he just couldn't keep up with his younger teammate. This is disastrous for Russell. Beyond embarrassing. And I know that his campaign hasn't exactly been trouble-free, but still.
What did we just witness? It's one of two scenarios. We either just witnessed the equivalent of Leicester City winning the Premier League in 2015/16. An outlier that's unlikely to happen again for the next several decades. Or we just witnessed the equivalent of a young Valentino Rossi re-spawning into the body of a Formula 1 driver. Rossi also won his first 500cc/MotoGP title in his second year, winning 11 out of 16 races.
The parallels don't stop there. Rossi had to outclass several multi-time champions on his way to the crown. He had to fight off the likes of Max Biaggi and Kenny Roberts Jr. Same as Kimi in his fight against Max and Lewis. Lando counts too. There's a certain "Rossi-esque" psychological quality to Antonelli, and I'm more than happy to admit that.
Photo: Mercedes-AMG F1 Team/Getty Images Let's hear from the man himself: "It’s difficult to put into words what I’m feeling right now. I’m still trying to process it all, but to be able to say that I am world champion is just incredible. This is a moment that I will remember for the rest of my life."
"I wouldn’t be here without this team and without all the people and partners who have supported me throughout my career. Mercedes has believed in me for so many years and given me this incredible opportunity, so to repay that trust by winning the World Championship together means so much. I also have to thank my family, my friends and everyone who has been there for me along the way."
Going into the 2027 season, I'll be more than happy to root for him earning back-to-back titles. However, I'd like to see Mercedes do a better job of giving Russell all the support he needs. I'm also rooting for Charles to get his first title. He's more than good enough.

Nissan’s “smoothest, quietest and quickest Rogue ever” arrived at United States dealerships at the end of October, and is getting ready to make its public debut at the Los Angeles Auto Show between November 20 and 29. But someone thought that since Nissan timed the release with Halloween, they should have also cooked an all-black Midnight Edition for the occasion, too.
The Japanese automaker is selling two different versions of its popular Rogue nameplate – the regular compact crossover SUV is still stuck on the T33 tier for the 2027 model year, but its Rogue Hybrid sibling has already made the switch to the T34 fourth edition lifestyle for the 2027MY. Nissan has announced that their all-new 2027 Rogue Hybrid went on sale in the United States on October 30, just a day prior to Halloween 2026.
“Rogue Hybrid is the next step in Nissan’s U.S. growth story. We set out to build the best hybrid to grow the brand, and Rogue Hybrid delivers with the efficiency, performance and refinement customers want,” said Tiago Castro, senior vice president, U.S. Marketing & Sales, Nissan and Infiniti. The model has a fuel economy of EPA-estimated 38 mpg combined, and it’s powered by the unconventional e-Power system, which, unlike conventional hybrids, uses the gasoline engine solely as a generator while the wheels are always driven by the dual electric motors.
Unlike the regular, older 2027 Nissan Rogue, which is available in S, SV, Dark Armor, Rock Creek, and Platinum grades, the all-new 2027 Rogue Hybrid only has three versions to show off: SV, SR, and Platinum. Actually, the new model only launches with the all-wheel-drive SR with the SR Technology Package, with the full model range set to become available in early 2027.
No worries, as those who seek more options have a solution thanks to the rumor mill and the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI. More precisely, good folks over at the " AutoYa " info channel on YouTube have unofficially imagined the CGI look of the all-new 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid with Midnight attire – since the Japanese automaker’s local division launched the model on the eve of Halloween 2026.

A fresh FDA review for Biohaven’s embattled ataxia drug lifted the biotech’s shares, while a late-stage lung cancer miss battered ArriVent, which failed to rebound even after encouraging early ADC data.
A renewed regulatory opening and a clinical setback sent two biotech stocks in opposite directions in October. Biohaven gained ground after the FDA agreed to review its rare disease resubmission, while ArriVent BioPharma plunged after its lead candidate missed in a Phase 3 cancer study, then suffered another selloff despite encouraging early results for a separate asset.
Here, BioSpace analyzes these two sizeable stock shifts and the developments driving the activity. This monthly series is not intended to be a comprehensive review of all public biotech movement.
Who’s hot: Biohaven (BHVN)
The FDA has accepted Biohaven’s twice-rebuffed rare disease drug for review, a regulatory decision that sent the biotech’s stock up at least 25% in late October.
It’s been a rocky road for troriluzole, Biohaven’s investigational treatment for spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA), a group of rare diseases that lead to the progressive loss of control over movement. In 2023, the FDA refused to even review Biohaven’s new drug application based on a Phase 3 trial that missed its primary endpoint.
More recently, in November 2025—after a three-month delay—the FDA rejected troriluzole, also known as Vyglxia, in SCA. In the complete response letter, the regulator cited concerns “inherent to real-world evidence and external control studies.” At the time, Biohaven’s stock halved and, on the heels of the rebuff, the company launched a sweeping cost-optimization initiative to maximize its resources.
But now the FDA has accepted the company’s resubmission for review and assigned a new target action date sometime in the first quarter of 2027, according to an Oct. 22 SEC filing . The agency also plans to hold an advisory committee meeting for the application, with an adcomm date expected to be set “in the near term,” according to the document.
“Ultimately, we would expect Biohaven shares to re-rate if there is a clear path to approval here for Vyglxia given a blockbuster orphan disease opportunity across all SCA genotypes,” William Blair analysts wrote Oct. 22.
Who’s not: Arrivent BioPharma (AVBP)
ArriVent BioPharma’s stock halved after its tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) failed to improve progression-free survival (PFS) rates in a Phase 3 lung cancer trial. The biotech’s stock has yet to recover, falling further even after early “promising” data for a separate asset at this year’s European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) meeting in Spain.
In the first week of October, Arrivent shared open-label data for its most advanced asset, firmonertinib, an EGFR TKI designed to penetrate the brain. The Allist Pharmaceuticals–partnered candidate demonstrated a median PFS of 11 months in certain non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) populations, as compared to 9.5 months for patients on chemotherapy—a finding that wasn’t statistically significant.
Truist analysts viewed the miss as largely driven by the stronger-than-expected PFS seen in the control group, up from an expected seven months.
The trial results sent ArriVent’s stock plummeting nearly 50% on Oct. 6, from $28.46 to $12.09 at market close.
Analysts have turned their focus to a late-stage test of firmonertinib in a different type of lung cancer and the biotech’s antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) pipeline, including ARR-217, an ADC ArriVent is developing alongside Lepu Biopharma for colorectal and gastrointestinal cancers.
Early data for the asset were presented as a late-breaker at ESMO last week. The Phase 1 data slice demonstrated a 44.8% preliminary objective response rate among patients with metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC).
While Truist found the early findings “encouraging,” displaying “emerging durability, with favorable tolerability,” it didn’t stop investors from sending the biotech’s stock down about 27% that day. Truist deemed the stock drop “disproportionate” and “disconnected” to the ARR-217 data.
“We believe today’s weakness instead reflects plausible profit-taking following the stock’s ~39% recovery from its October 6 close through Friday,” Truist wrote in an Oct. 26 note, while also citing “a high differentiation bar in the crowded mCRC ADC landscape.”
ArriVent is expected to share Phase 1b data for the asset in the first half of next year, which will provide clarity on its development path, according to Truist. The analyst modeled peak sales of $850 million for ARR-217 and has started including it in the company’s valuation.
“Firmonertinib clarity is expected in 1Q27, but ARR-217 begins to rebalance the story,” the analysts wrote.

Companies that have faced a cyber attack are now increasingly likely to face lawsuits too, from customers or staff over any breach of data security.
JB Hunt is the latest: it is facing four proposed class actions, after a cybercrime group claimed to have taken employee information and millions of business records from the US transport and logistics company.
The suits, filed in the Western District of Arkansas on 27 and 28 October, allege JB Hunt failed to protect employees’ personal information. Named plaintiffs include current and former workers. The claims have not been tested in court, and no class has yet been certified.
Cyber attacks often leave logistics companies facing litigation beyond the immediate cost of restoring systems. Motor carriers sued freight broker TQL after a breach exposed business information, while employees and applicants brought claims against cold-chain operator Americold over compromised personal data. Expeditors has also faced claims from customers alleging losses after a 2022 attack disrupted services.
The JB Hunt attacker, calling itself WhiteArmor, posted its claim on or about 23 October, although it is not clear exactly when the hack took place. The complainants repeat its claim to hold 140,838 employee records for a $5m ransom.
One complaint also lists what WhiteArmor claims to hold: 1.7m carrier contacts, 38.2m invoices, 973 Microsoft 365 mailboxes, and records concerning 374,000 organisations. JB Hunt has not confirmed what information was accessed or how many people were affected.
JB Hunt has acknowledged an incident took place, while stressing that freight operations have continued. A spokesperson reportedly told local media it was investigating “unauthorised access to certain information within an isolated portion” of its technology system.
“Our systems remain operational, and there has been no disruption to our ability to serve customers,” the spokesperson said. JB Hunt added it had brought in a cybersecurity firm, notified law enforcement, and revoked the unauthorised access.
The lawsuits allege inadequate data security and seek damages and changes to the company’s security practices. Aaron Hunter, a former employee, said in his complaint that he had received no individual breach notice as of 27 October , when he filed his complaint.
For shippers and carriers, the unanswered question is whether any commercially sensitive information was accessed. The business data figures cited in the lawsuits are the hackers’ assertions, while the legal claims filed so far focus on employees’ personal information.
Following a 2022 cyber attack that shut down most of Expeditors’ operating systems, customers including iRobot and POC USA sued the forwarder over alleged losses from interrupted warehousing and deliveries. JB Hunt says its ability to serve customers has not been disrupted and the lawsuits do not allege any losses from halted freight movements.
Check out today’s podcasts: News in Brief, focusing on ocean freight with Xeneta’s Peter Sand ; and a bonus episode: news from TIACA ‘s Air Cargo Forum in Miami.

Flexport’s freight volumes are up 40% from a year ago while its headcount has grown 5%, founder and CEO Ryan Petersen told FreightWaves. He credits the gap to artificial intelligence tools the company now runs across customs, routing and its own engineering teams.
The AI has a limit in customs, the most regulated part of Flexport’s business. There, an AI-generated tariff code still has to pass a licensed broker before it can legally reach U.S. Customs and Border Protection.
“Our volumes are up 40% annually. And headcount’s only up 5%, so you can see the AI’s working,” Petersen said.
The interview followed Flexport’s fall technology release , which added an AI classification tool to its customs software and rail, barge and air routing to its free Flexport Atlas map. Time magazine named Flexport’s Customs Technology Suite to its Best Inventions of 2026 list on Oct. 15.
AI classification still needs a licensed broker
Classifying goods under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule is “the hardest problem in customs,” Petersen said. Flexport’s new tool suggests a 10-digit code and links the CBP rulings behind it.
Federal law limits who can do that work for someone else. In a Jan. 16 ruling , CBP found that a foreign online platform was conducting customs business when its AI tool derived tariff subheadings beyond the six-digit level for goods that would be entered. Under 19 U.S.C. 1641, only a licensed customs broker can conduct customs business on behalf of another party.
Any AI-suggested code a customer wants to use goes to a licensed customs broker on Flexport’s team, who reviews it by hand before filing. “It’s kind of like how AI meets the real world,” Petersen said.
AI models hallucinate often in customs work, he said, partly because CBP leaves its binding rulings on specific products posted after newer ones supersede them.
“They don’t delete the old one. They’re both there,” Petersen said. An AI model can cite the outdated ruling, he said, where an experienced broker would know to ignore it.
Flexport says audits found 20% error rate at rivals
In February, Flexport launched a free tool that lets any company audit its customs broker’s past entries . Petersen called it “probably the meanest thing we’ve ever built.”
Audits of entries filed by competing brokers found an average error rate of 20%, he said. He blamed the errors on 2025’s tariff churn.
Flexport’s own error rate on U.S. customs filings last year was 0.2%, which Petersen put at about 100 times better.
That comparison has grown since February, when Petersen estimated the 0.2% rate was a 100X improvement over any other broker. Flexport’s release said that estimate was “based on what we know of other customs brokers.”
A tariff database has to be updated regularly by experts who follow rule changes, Petersen said. Flexport offers its tariff simulator free to the public and builds the same data into the workflow its brokers use to clear entries.
At some point, Petersen said, an importer that isn’t using Flexport’s tariff technology is close to negligent.
AI writes code for customer rules
Flexport also keeps AI from acting alone on customer rules. Logistics customers set their own delivery rules, Petersen said, such as notice 10 days ahead for one warehouse and three days ahead for another.
Petersen called the rules “a spaghetti web of business logic.” Customers are valuable enough that a forwarder follows whatever rules they set, he said.
AI alone can’t be trusted to follow those rules consistently, he said. “If it misses, the misses are worth too much.”
So Flexport has AI write code for those rules. Once an expert signs off, the code runs the same way every time.
Petersen ties ocean demand to tariff refunds
Flexport’s ocean peak started early this year, Petersen said: “Basically since April, we’ve been just ripping.”
Flexport first read the surge as an early peak season, Petersen said. Customers are still booking cargo that won’t arrive before Christmas, so he now counts it as growth.
Petersen has a theory for the demand that he said he hasn’t seen written anywhere: tariff refunds. The Supreme Court struck down tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act in February. As of Oct. 2, CBP had sent about $126 billion in refunds to the Treasury Department for disbursement, Supply Chain Dive reported , citing a court filing.
Petersen called the refunds a “massive stimulus for the industry” that companies hadn’t planned for.
Customers have told him they plan to spend the money on more inventory, he said, and many have been short on capital for a long time.
“Most lottery winners go bankrupt,” Petersen said he tells customers. “Don’t go crazy buying inventory.”
Supply matters too, Petersen said. Only 10 or 11 ocean carriers remain, and they have gotten better at controlling capacity by slowing ships and canceling sailings.
Freightos’ Oct. 20 weekly update put Asia-U.S. West Coast rates at $8,126 per 40-foot container and East Coast rates at $9,700, calling trans-Pacific prices “stable but still highly elevated” even as volumes are expected to cool. FreightWaves noted in September that those rates remain well below their 2021 highs.
Data center cargo fills air freight
On ocean freight, Petersen said he makes “zero market predictions.” He is watching air freight, where he estimated that data center cargo, from chips and server racks to construction materials, accounts for around 8% of global capacity. He said it is projected to triple next year, and lanes from Taiwan and Southeast Asia to the U.S. will be “really constrained.”
An air freight expert at Flexport’s conference put the number of full freighters flying from Taiwan to the U.S. just for data centers at 30 a day, Petersen said.
A single freighter can carry cargo worth as much as $500 million when it is all GPUs and server racks, he said. Waiting 30 days for an ocean crossing would add interest on that cargo and delay revenue from the finished data center.
That cargo will move by air “probably forever,” he said.
The data center surge has moved air rates less than Petersen expected. New capacity is part of the reason, he said: Middle Eastern airlines are returning planes to service and have bought more cargo aircraft.
Smaller teams, bigger AI budgets
AI is also changing how Flexport organizes engineers. The company is weighing teams of two or three engineers, down from a standard of eight, Petersen said. Atlas started as a one-engineer project, he said.
Companies worried about what AI tokens cost should spend more, Petersen said, since he estimates the tools make an engineer seven times more efficient.
Flexport has held two large technology releases a year for the past two years, and the fall release was its fourth on that schedule. Petersen said the company may move to three or four releases in 2027 because of how fast its teams are building.
He is not worried that AI model makers will move into freight.
“The frontier companies are not going to become a logistics provider,” Petersen said. “We just have to be super aggressive in using them to make our business amazing, keep adding new products, extending what we do.”
Why it matters: Flexport credits AI for 40% volume growth on 5% more staff. In customs, its AI still routes through licensed brokers, as CBP rules require, and the 20% error rate it cites for competitors comes from its own audits.

Iconic JDM Sat 28 Years in Barn, Owner's Family Lets It Go at Less Than Half Price, Revival Incoming
63 photos
Photo: YouTube/WD Detailing
Produced between 1983 and 2000 across two distinct generations, the Nissan 300ZX carried the Japanese automaker's Z-car sports coupe lineage from the analog 1980s into the high-tech 1990s. Known as the Fairlady Z in its home market, the 300ZX earned a permanent seat at the table of 1990s Japanese performance royalty alongside the Nissan Skyline GT-R, the fourth-generation Toyota Supra, the Mazda RX-7, and the aluminum-bodied mid-engine Honda NSX.
While the Toyota Supra and Nissan Skyline GT-R later dominated popular culture through movie franchises and tuner-friendly inline-six engines capable of massive aftermarket output, the 300ZX carved a different legacy. Celebrated by period journalists as a technological tour de force with supercar styling, it remained slightly more niche in tuning circles only because its tightly packed V6 engine bay put off mechanics, making clean, unmolested survivors prized collector pieces today.
One such survivor is a yellow 1990 Nissan 300ZX 2+0 T-top coupe that spent 28 years hidden away inside a dark storage building after last seeing the road in 1998. To rescue the forgotten Japanese sports car and transform it into a daily driver, the Cleveland, Ohio specialists at WD Detailing, RJ Wagner, Brent DiCesare, and Mike Tudor, teamed up with YouTube’s most famous white racing helmet, the DIY automotive creator Chris Magello of the ChrisFix channel.
Although Magello has spent 16 years teaching millions how to maintain and repair vehicles while wearing his trademark white racing helmet, this 1990 Z32 marked his very first barn-find project. Yes, after nearly two BILLION YouTube views, the car nut still has new things to do, learn, and teach.
Photo: YouTube/WD Detailing He spotted the 106,000-mile (170,590-kilometer) 5-speed manual coupe through AutoTempest on an eBay estate sale listing that included only three photos, a $4,900 asking price, and a short note stating the car ran when parked in 1998.
Moving quickly, Magello asked his friend Hussein Ashkanani from Forza Automotive to inspect the Nissan that same day. After checking 5-year price trends showing clean naturally aspirated Z32 coupes listed between $9,000 and $10,000 and selling for $7,000 to $8,000, Magello negotiated a $2,300 purchase price by promising to get it running again.
During the initial inspection, Hussein also revealed the dark, heartbreaking reason the sports car had been locked away.
Photo: YouTube/WD Detailing The woman selling the 300ZX had inherited it from her brother, who drove the car during the 1990s and ran a towing company. One night in 1998, he responded to a tow call, where the callers robbed and fatally shot him. Grief-stricken, his family parked the coupe inside their barn with its July 1998 Kentucky license plate, leaving it untouched on four flat tires until the YouTubers pulled it out for a f ull revival.
ChrisFix the 16-inch alloy wheels using rubber cleaner and iron-dissolving Purple Rain solution before the crew pressure-washed the engine bay and foamed the body with Cherry Suds. Hoisting the car on the lift, RJ put on a hazmat suit and racing helmet to degrease the undercarriage.
Inside the T-top cabin, Mike inspected the pod-style dashboard controls, door-mounted seat belts, and lifeless clutch pedal before pulling the seats, leaving Brent to treat the heavy carpet with Rust-Oleum rust dissolver and enzyme pre-soak. Once the car was nice and shiny, the livery got a thorough polish before the new owner took it to his shop for a mechanical overhaul (to be featured on his YouTube channel).
Photo: YouTube/WD Detailing Competing in the front-engine, rear-wheel-drive sports car and grand tourer segment, the Nissan 300ZX spanned two generations: the Z31 built from 1983 to 1989 and the Z32 produced from 1989 to 2000. Offered with 5-speed manual or 4-speed automatic transmissions, the Z31 replaced earlier inline-sixes with Japan's first mass-produced V6 engines, alongside a pair of Japanese-market 2.0-liter engines - an inline-six and a turbo V6 rated at 170 PS (168 hp).
In export markets, the first-generation Z31 launched for 1984 with the naturally aspirated 3.0-liter SOHC 12-valve V6, delivering 160 hp (162 PS) and 173 lb-ft (235 Nm) of torque for an 8.6-second 0 to 60 mph (97 kph) run and a 134 mph (216 kph) top speed. Conversely, the pinnacle Z32 engine was the 3.0-liter DOHC 24-valve twin-turbocharged V6, packing dual intercoolers and variable valve timing.
That flagship powerplant generated 300 hp (304 PS) at 6,400 rpm and 283 lb-ft (384 Nm) of torque at 3,600 rpm, launching the Z32 Twin Turbo from 0 to 60 mph (97 kph) in 5.0 seconds, through the quarter-mile in 13.7 seconds at 101 mph (163 kph), and to a limited 155 mph (250 kph) top speed. Out of roughly 270,000 Z32 units built globally, North America received approximately 83,000 cars.
Photo: YouTube/WD Detailing Magello's 1990 model hails from the Z32's inaugural and highest-selling North American season, which accounted for 39,290 units and earned Motor Trend's Import Car of the Year award. Measuring 169.5 inches (4,305 millimeters) long on a 96.5-inch (2,451-millimeter) wheelbase and weighing 3,219 lbs (1,460 kg), the 1990 300ZX coupe houses the naturally aspirated 3.0-liter (2,960-cc) DOHC 24-valve V6 producing 222 hp (225 PS) and 198 lb-ft (268 Nm).
Paired with its factory 5-speed manual gearbox and four-wheel independent multi-link suspension, the 1990 naturally aspirated coupe reaches 60 mph (97 kph) in 7.0 seconds, covers the quarter-mile in 15.5 seconds at 91 mph (146 kph), and hits a 146 mph (235 kph) top speed. Now gleaming after its WD Detailing revival, this 1990 300ZX is ready for Magello's wrenching to return to the streets after 28 years.

Photo: Wheels / YouTube
The R35 Nissan GT-R has been around since December 2007, and nobody was ultimately surprised when it bowed out from production last summer. But the C8 generation of the iconic Chevrolet Corvette is much younger and, surprisingly, it already has defunct versions – well, one, that is.
The Japanese grand tourer – aka Godzilla for enthusiasts – had a long stint, surviving the massive changes across the sports car market for almost 18 years. It had a long, clean, and very good run, and we’re not surprised if some folks already consider it a legend among its peers.
On the other hand, the C8 debuted back in 2019 with the biggest change a Chevrolet Corvette had ever seen – it switched from a classic front-engine RWD format to the mid-engine setup. It also gained, for the first time, all-wheel drive and a performance hybrid powertrain, all courtesy of the newly introduced E-Ray version.
However, it was a short-lived premiere, and for the 2027 model year General Motors introduced a brand-new 6.7-liter V8 engine used for the base Stingray along with the returning Grand Sport and the first-ever Grand Sport X. While the former two have 535 hp and 520 lb-ft of torque both, the third option gained the ZR1X’s electrified setup and together with the new V8 churns out 721 hp, much more than E-Ray’s previous 655 combined horsepower.
Nevertheless, a C8 Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray is never an opponent that should be trifled with, since it has AWD and can launch like a rocket thanks to its hybrid setup. Well, the videographer behind the ' Wheels ' channel on YouTube recently took a detour around Bradenton Motorsports Park in Florida for the local FL2K competition, and showed us a feisty America versus Import brawl thanks to the meeting between a crimson R35 Nissan GT-R and a Hysteria Purple E-Ray.
We don’t know if both cars are stock, though it’s pretty obvious that either driver has opted at least for a beefier track tire and wheel setup. Well, as it turns out, the R35 Nissan GT-R simply destroyed the all-wheel-drive and hybrid-assisted E-Ray right off the line – the driver’s reaction time was absolutely bonkers (0.02!).
The car wasn’t any less, either, as it raised its nose and kept it up while accelerating like there’s no tomorrow, leaving the Corvette far behind. In the end, the difference was pretty obvious: 10.49s for the E-Ray at 126 mph while the Godzilla crossed the line at BMP in just 8.31s and at a lower trap speed of 121 mph.
So, what do you think? Are you eagerly awaiting the next-generation Nissan GT-R, which could also be a performance hybrid just like the E-Ray? Maybe we’ll see the R36 in a clash with the more powerful C8 Grand Sport X in the not-so-distant future…

Ducati Monster Dark Is an All-Black Back-to-Basics Naked Meant for Purists
7 photos
Photo: Ducati
The last time we heard anything about Ducati's iconic Monster bike was back in the spring of this year, when the Italians brought forth a variant called the Sport. While that one was supposed to honor the S4, the first-ever four-valve Ducati Monster, the latest addition to the range, the Dark, kind of tries to get back to the basics, and to a time that made the model known to the world as a bike for purists.
The Monster is currently in its fifth generation, which broke cover in February 2026. The newcomer is now joining the range as everything you need, and nothing more, in the words of Ducati itself.
Mechanically speaking, the Dark doesn't bring novelties to the table. The aluminum monocoque frame holds the same 890cc V2 engine with variable valve timing as the rest of the range, with the same performance levels: 111 hp at 9,000 rpm and 91 Nm of torque at 7,250 rpm.
The numbers mean even more if you put them in the proper context. Just consider this: the Ducati Monster Dark tips the scales at just 386 pounds (175 kg, curb weight), almost nine pounds (four kg) lighter than the previous generation.
The bike's suspension system continues to be supplied by specialist Showa, and it consists of a 43 mm upside-down fork at the front and a shock absorber with preload adjustment at the rear.
The tech ties into the standard wheels of the model, only painted completely black for the Dark and shod in Pirelli Diablo Rosso IV tires. Brembo braking hardware takes care of the bike's stopping needs.
What makes the Dark special, then, other than its black wheels? Well, first and foremost, we've got the total black livery, contrasted as much as it can be by the unpainted exhaust end caps and snorkel.
A single-material seat for rider and passenger, located 815 mm off the ground, is mounted on the frame, while further to the front the bike's bison-back fuel tank frames the headlight with its shoulders. All of this, says Ducati , is meant to make the Dark look and feel like the original Monster from back in the early 1990s.
The Italians say the motorcycle will become available at dealers starting this month, with pricing for the UK market having been set at £10,995, including VAT (that's $14,750 at today's exchange rates). Ducati says this is the special launch price, hinting that it could go up a bit in the near future.
There are hopes that both experienced riders and noobs will be drawn to the model, especially those looking for a pure expression of the two-wheeler. As always, the naked Ducati Monster Dark will also be available as a detuned version for European A2 license holders.

1994 Williams FW16 Driven by Ayrton Senna in His Final Season Is Up for Grabs for the First Time
14 photos
Photo: RM Sotheby's
I'm not entirely sure why that is so, but the past few weeks have seen an unprecedented number of vehicles somehow tied to Formula 1 legend Ayrton Senna come to light. First, the Honda NSX the Brazilian used while in Europe, then a couple of 1991 McLaren MP4/6A racers, and now a Williams FW16.
Of these four cars, the Williams is perhaps the one with the best story. Not only because it was born the same year the legendary driver passed, but because it was driven by the man in his final months on planet Earth, and it then entered the possession of his family, who kept it for three decades.
The race car I'm talking about is one of two surviving Williams FW16s driven by Senna, chassis FW16B-01. The car was not driven by the man in actual races, only during warm-up and testing, but that probably doesn't decrease its value in the slightest.
Senna climbed on board the racer at Interlagos and Jerez, with the car covering a total distance of 523 miles (842 km) between the two tracks . Following Senna's fatal crash in San Marino, the F1 car was updated and continued to serve the needs of the Williams crew.
It's what happened after the season ended that brings a lot of value to the car. You see, when Senna joined the team at the end of 1993, the team made him a promise that, should Williams win the 1994 Constructors’ World Championship, the driver would be gifted a chassis.
The team won the championship that year, but Senna was no longer around to receive the car. So Williams did the next best thing and gifted the car to the Brazilian's family. They held on to it for exactly 30 years.
Chassis FW16B-01 was sold for the first time to an undisclosed person back in 2024, during a private sale. As such, we don't know how much the buyer paid for it, but we do know that now, for the first time through a public auction, the current owner hopes to get as much as $6 million for it.
The car, unrestored and all original, is going under the RM Sotheby’s hammer later this month in New York, betting not only on its connection to the three-time Formula 1 champion, but also on the fact that, throughout 1994, it was also driven by other greats of this sport, including Nigel Mansell, Damon Hill, and David Coulthard.
As a fine touch, the car is selling with a little extra: the personal seat of the Brazilian driver. It remains to be seen if the right crowd is in the house when the hammer falls – naturally, we'll keep an eye on things and report back once we know more.

All-New Toyota Century Coupe Luxury Grand Tourer Gets Rendered in All-Black Production Guise Attire
9 photos
Photo: kelsonik / Instagram
Since Toyota Motor Corporation is the world’s best-selling automaker and also the most valuable representative of the automotive industry, it can allow itself to dream big in all sorts of directions.
TMC’s lofty targets for electric fuel cell models are well known, along with the fact that they never materialized, for example. But they have other ideas, too, like Gazoo Racing becoming an independent brand all over again and establishing itself with the upcoming GR GT hybrid V8 sports car. But that’s not all, of course.
Worldwide, the most renowned TMC brands are the namesake Toyota and the premium Lexus division, but a little more than a year ago Toyota debuted its former Century nameplate as a standalone brand at the 2025 Japan Mobility Show, taking a page out of Hyundai and Genesis’ playbook in the process.
Initially and for decades on end, the Toyota Century was the most luxurious car ever created in Japan – debuting in sedan form in 1967 and mostly reserved for domestic sales to government officials and major business elites. It mostly remained the same for decades – until in 2023, when it also gained an SUV sibling.
Now, the shift is even more pronounced because the Century has become a stand-alone brand that will reign on top of all TMC offerings on par with the likes of Rolls-Royce or Bentley. They announced the split with a slightly high-riding Century grand tourer coupe concept that looked ready to take on the Bentley Continental GT or the Rolls-Royce Spectre at a moment’s notice.
Of course, these things take time to develop, and the last time we heard anything about Century it was in October 2026 when Toyota looked to make its new Century brand a global asset, as the plug-in hybrid V6-powered Century SUV has expanded to China and to other countries in Asia and the Middle East in very small volumes.
Now, the Century brand has also caught the attention of a member of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators who stopped dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI and took another look at the striking Century high-riding coupe concept introduced last year.
More precisely, Nikita Chuicko, the virtual artist better known as " kelsonik " on social media, thinks that now is the right CGI time to work on making the dreams of Toyota entirely possible with a production version of the Century grand tourer. It’s dressed in all-black attire now and keeps most of the prototype’s design traits while also looking ready for series production – and it even gains a set of deeply concave black alloy wheels courtesy of the aftermarket realm in the CGI process.
Also, the pixel master doesn’t let it alone across the plains of Imagination Land – they showcase it back-to-back with the competition, a Bentley Continental GT feeling a bit blue about itself or green with envy, but also compared to the real world’s concept car.
