The rapid adoption and use of artificial intelligence is having a transformative effect on GPU designs, with accelerators nowadays being optimized for lower-precision formats such as FP16, BF16, and FP8 since these formats provide the computational throughput required for both AI training and inference.
However, many traditional high-performance computing (HPC) applications have to use FP64 (double-precision) arithmetic to ensure numerical accuracy, stability, and convergence. This presents a problem for organizations that wish to support both AI and scientific computing on shared accelerator infrastructure.
Fortunately, organizations do not have to choose between AI acceleration and native FP64 performance.
Why Native FP64 Performance Remains Essential
AMD Instinct MI430X
FP64 remains necessary for many demanding scientific applications, such as quantum chemistry, molecular simulations, electromagnetic simulations, computational physics, and numerical linear algebra; in large-scale iterative and direct solvers, small numerical errors can build up and affect convergence and, in some cases, spoil the simulation results.
While some applications can use mixed precision to boost performance, others need double precision for most calculations.
Methods like Ozaki emulation let organizations use lower-precision hardware to run higher-precision calculations. However, they cannot serve as universal replacements for native FP64 capabilities.
Understanding Ozaki Emulation and its Performance Limitations
The Ozaki method achieves higher-precision matrix calculations through a series of lower-precision operations. It breaks down high-precision values into lower-precision components, processes them using high-throughput hardware, and then combines the results to achieve the required accuracy.
This method is appealing because modern AI accelerators provide excellent throughput at lower precision. For certain dense linear algebra operations, Ozaki emulation can reach FP64 accuracy. This does not mean it reproduces all the numerical properties of native IEEE FP64 arithmetic.
Although it has potential, Ozaki emulation involves trade-offs that can limit application-level performance.
Computational overhead is a major issue. While native FP64 hardware can carry out double-precision operations directly, Ozaki emulation must perform several calculations at lower precision and include extra accumulation steps. Depending on the required accuracy and the decomposition methods used, this extra work can considerably reduce the performance benefit of lower-precision hardware.
Memory and data movement also pose challenges. When values are broken down and intermediate results are stored, the demand on memory capacity, bandwidth, and cache resources rises. In memory-bound high-performance computing applications, this data movement can cancel out improvements in computational throughput.
Workload suitability is also important. Dense matrix multiplication can use optimized matrix engines and efficient data reuse, while sparse computations, irregular memory accesses, and communication-intensive applications may achieve only much smaller gains.
Ultimately, the degree of numerical accuracy depends on the decomposition methods, precision formats, and accumulation strategies; since different implementations can produce different error characteristics, validation must be specific to each application.
Native FP64 Versus Emulation: Evaluating Real-World Performance
To compare native FP64 with emulated precision, users must look beyond peak arithmetic performance.
An accelerator that has very high FP16 or BF16 throughput might seem to beat native FP64 hardware when using emulation. Still, such a comparison can be deceptive if it ignores decomposition overhead, extra memory traffic, substantial additional memory capacity requirements, and the cost of achieving the necessary numerical accuracy.
Organizations should use application-level benchmarks to assess both methods, the benchmarks being those that measure sustained throughput, time to solution, memory utilization, communication overhead, and energy efficiency.
Numerical accuracy and convergence are equally important; a matrix multiplication kernel that attains FP64-equivalent accuracy under certain conditions does not ensure that the whole scientific application will exhibit the same numerical behavior.
A simple example puts these issues into perspective. When emulating a double-precision floating-point matrix calculation, the “base” memory (i.e., the memory required when using hardware FP64) can be computed by taking the matrix size, multiplying it by itself, and then by 3 and then by 8 bytes. For a matrix size of 4,096, hardware FP64 would then need (4096^2)*3*8 bytes, which is 384MB. The extra memory needed to get full accuracy using software emulation would be about 849 MB. This means that instead of 384 MB of storage, emulation would take 384 + 849, or roughly 3.21x more memory than HW FP64.
If the matrix size is larger, say 32,768, the required base storage would be 24 GB, and emulation would need 52 extra GB (3.17x more storage).
Energy consumption also matters; depending on the hardware and workload, more lower-precision operations can use more energy than fewer native FP64 operations.
Bottom line: Ozaki emulation is valuable when the throughput benefits of reduced precision outweigh its overhead. Native FP64, on the other hand, provides a more robust way to run applications with extensive double-precision needs.
AMD’s Approach: Native FP64 Performance Without Mandatory Emulation
AMD’s architecture supports demanding scientific workloads alongside emerging AI applications.
AMD Instinct™ GPUs offer native FP64 support, enabling HPC applications to run double-precision operations without special emulation. Moreover, lower-precision formats let organizations speed up AI and mixed-precision workloads.
Its flexibility means applications can choose the level of precision that matches their requirements rather than being constrained by the hardware.
Another important factor to take into account is the software ecosystem. AMD ROCm™ is an open software platform for GPU computing which includes compilers, development tools, and optimized numerical libraries. These features enable organizations to port, develop, and optimize scientific applications while using native FP64 and lower-precision acceleration.
EDA: An Illustrative Example
The value of this approach can be seen in electronic design automation (EDA). Semiconductor design workflows include computationally intensive tasks such as circuit simulation, electromagnetic analysis, power integrity analysis, and numerical optimization.
Because many of these applications rely on precise numerical calculations, large sparse systems, and iterative solvers, numerical stability and convergence are essential to reliable results.
Native FP64 execution can be used for these workloads to avoid the overhead and implementation complexity of precision emulation. Furthermore, high memory bandwidth and capacity help handle the large, irregular datasets encountered in EDA simulations.
At the same time, lower-precision acceleration can benefit AI-assisted design optimization and other new EDA techniques; by supporting both capabilities on the same accelerator platform, semiconductor companies gain more flexibility to run either traditional simulation or AI-improved design processes.
A Final Word: Precision Flexibility Will Define Future HPC Systems
Ozaki emulation shows how innovative numerical techniques can increase the usefulness of lower-precision AI accelerators. For appropriate workloads, it provides a valuable way to use high-throughput matrix hardware.
Its effectiveness depends on workload characteristics, numerical requirements, and computational overhead; therefore, it cannot be used everywhere as a substitute for native double-precision arithmetic.
As AI and traditional HPC systems converge, organizations will need accelerator architectures that can efficiently support multiple precision formats.
For any organization experiencing these problems, the most important thing is to choose systems that deliver reliable application-level performance without unnecessary concessions in precision. Native FP64 will still be essential to achieving this objective.
To learn more about FP64 Performance of AMD Instinct products and the Limits of Ozaki Emulation, visit the AMD booth #3028 at SC26.
